analysis.one_liner: Boosts Social Security benefits and funds it by phasing out the payroll tax cap on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill to lift the Social Security payroll tax cap and base cost-of-living raises on seniors' actual expenses died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change Social Security in three main ways: it would base annual cost-of-living raises on an index that tracks what people 62 and older actually spend money on (medical care and housing, which rise faster than the current index), it would gradually remove the cap that exempts income above roughly $147,000 a year from Social Security taxes, and it would pay a surviving family the Social Security benefit for the month a beneficiary dies, which current law does not do. High earners who pay into the system above the cap would also earn somewhat larger benefits on those earnings.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security retirees and disabled beneficiaries, whose annual raises would track senior-specific costs; and families of beneficiaries, who would receive a prorated payment for the month of a beneficiary's death. High earners would pay more in payroll taxes but would also accrue additional benefit credit on those earnings.

how_it_helps.text: Cost-of-living adjustments would be calculated using a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which weights the medical and housing costs typical of people 62 and older, rather than the general index [S2][S3].

The bill phases out the exemption of wages above the contribution and benefit base from Social Security taxes over six years, so that by 2029 all earnings are taxed; it applies the same phase-down to self-employment income [S3].
Benefits would be paid through the month of a beneficiary's death, prorated by days, payable to the estate or a named payee — closing a gap where the final month's check is lost [S3].

The bill contains a formula change (preventing an unintended benefit drop tied to the national average wage index) and credit for high earners' above-cap earnings in the benefit formula, so the new taxes translate into higher benefits for those who pay them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners — people with wages or self-employment income above the annual contribution and benefit base (about $147,000 in 2022) — who would pay the 12.4% Social Security tax on income that is currently exempt, phased in fully by 2029. The federal government would bear higher benefit payments, offset by the new tax revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the payroll tax cap

drawbacks.text: It is a large tax increase on high earners and on higher-earning self-employed people and small-business owners, phasing in from 86% of above-cap earnings taxed in 2023 to 100% after 2028 [S3].

Using a senior-specific price index would produce larger annual increases in most years, raising the program's long-term cost; the bill pairs the tax increase with expanded benefits rather than directing all new revenue to solvency [S2][S3].

High earners do receive added benefit credit on their newly taxed earnings, but at low accrual rates (3% and 0.25% marginal factors), so their tax increase would substantially exceed their added benefits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit changes are modest, targeted improvements — a more accurate inflation measure for retirees and a death-month payment fix — paid for by a significant, explicitly identified tax increase on high-income earners. The design is coherent: new revenue is tied to new benefit credit. The tradeoff is real but one-sided: the cost lands on a small group of high earners while the gains spread across tens of millions of beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2022 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Hirono introduced the bill with Senators Smith and Merkley on July 21, 2022 [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — is recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners are better off: the payroll tax on income above the cap never took effect. The current Social Security benefit and inflation formulas remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the tax cap

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to the Finance Committee

for.name: Sens. Tina Smith and Jeff Merkley

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 21, 2022 and took no recorded action before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties stood; no Republican cosponsor joined.

industries.note: The bill phases out the exemption of income above the payroll tax cap, subjecting earnings above roughly $147,000 to the 12.4% Social Security tax. Their added benefit credit is small relative to the new taxes.

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals and owners of pass-through businesses
industries.note: The same phase-down applies to net earnings from self-employment, so higher-earning independent professionals and small-business owners would see their self-employment tax base expand to all earnings by 2029.
